data.title: What are the main events for today?
data.description:
EUROPEAN SESSION

In the European session, the main highlight was the UK Retail Sales report. The data showed a strong rebound in October, beating expectations across both headline and underlying measures, with volumes rising 0.7% m/m and sales excluding autos and fuel increasing 0.9%. The recovery was broad-based, supported by stronger food and non-food sales, while online spending also continued to expand.

Although the figures point to resilient consumer demand, the three-month growth rate remained relatively modest at 0.4%. Overall, the report does little to change the Bank of England policy outlook, with markets already expecting a 25 bps rate hike in December.

data.title: Paulson tells Q&A the Fed has more tightening to do, after a speech with no rate steer
data.description:
Paulson’s comments confirm the hawkish lean that her prepared remarks left unsaid, which supports quarter-point December pricing and the view that hikes continue into 2027. Her emphasis on a deliberate pace argues against Waller’s 50 basis point idea, so the comments are more likely to firm up 2027 pricing than lift odds of a jumbo move. That combination supports front-end Treasury yields and the dollar. It’s another headwind for gold, which is already being sold toward $3,600.

---
Paulson’s speech offered no rate steer, but her answers to questions did: more hikes are coming, steadily rather than in a rush.

data.title: UBS cuts global stocks to Neutral, days after Morgan Stanley went maximum overweight
data.description:
The split between two tier-one houses underlines how finely balanced the 2027 equity case is. Concentration in AI-linked megacaps is the fault line. UBS’s preference for the Eurozone, equal-weight US strategies, industrials and health care points to rotation rather than outright selling, which could cushion broader indices even if tech leaders struggle. Higher-for-longer Fed rates and yields above 5% remain the key risk to valuations, so the December 9 Fed decision and the rate path into 2027 matter for both views. For Asia, where AI and chip stocks dominate several indices, UBS’s concentration warning is particularly relevant after Thursday's, now Friday’s, selloff.

---

data.title: No, the Fed isn’t pumping $1.756 billion into markets on Friday morning: what that viral post gets wrong
data.description:
These operations are pre-announced, small relative to the Treasury market and reserve-neutral, so they carry no policy signal. The real liquidity story is the Fed’s hiking path (eg. J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call ) and year-end funding conditions, where rising net bill supply, not these purchases, is the main influence on reserves. Traders watching for genuine balance sheet signals should focus on any change in the Desk’s language about reserve conditions, or a return of reserve management purchases.

---

data.title: A December BoJ hike may not be enough: why a fuzzy endpoint keeps yen bears circling
data.description:
With a December hike largely priced, the yen’s direction now hinges on the BoJ’s guidance beyond it. A vague statement or a cautious press conference from Ueda on December 18 risks a “hike and sell” reaction like last December’s. A clearer commitment to keep tightening toward 2% would give the yen more durable support. Until then, intervention risk near 160 is doing more to cap USD/JPY than rate expectations are. The July board changes add a longer-dated dovish tail risk that could weigh on yen forwards.

---
The BoJ is agreed on December but divided on the destination, and that missing endpoint may matter more to the yen than the hike itself.

data.title: No way back for oil after Hormuz, says IEA’s Birol, but Goldman still sees Brent at $78
data.description:
For oil, the two views point to a split between the structure of the market and the price. Long-dated risk premiums tied to Hormuz may persist as importers pay up for security of supply. Near-dated Brent faces pressure from a growing surplus and new bypass capacity. Brent’s muted reaction to fresh mine claims supports Goldman’s view that the market is becoming less sensitive to headlines from the strait. Diesel and jet fuel remain the tightest part of the complex, so refining margins could stay elevated even if crude eases. Importers in Asia carry the most exposure, given their heavy reliance on Gulf supply.

---

data.title: US envoys float NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for Donbas, WSJ reports
data.description:
The report shows active diplomacy but no convergence, so markets are unlikely to price a settlement soon. European defence stocks are the most headline-sensitive, and any sign of a breakthrough would test their rally. A credible peace path would eventually weigh on European gas prices and diesel cracks, where Russian refining and product exports have been a supply risk, and could support the euro. For oil, the Middle East remains the bigger driver, so Ukraine headlines are a secondary factor for crude itself.

---

data.title: ICYMI: AMD slides 8% as short seller Hunterbrook ties its firmware to a blacklisted Chinese firm
data.description:
The allegations add a legal and regulatory overhang to a stock already hit by tighter US export licensing this month. Commerce’s response, or silence, is now the key variable. The China and Singapore revenue figures give bears a concrete number to point to, which could keep pressure on AMD even without any enforcement action. For the wider sector, a second short-seller campaign on China ties raises the risk premium on US chipmakers with large Asian sales, adding to the selling already hitting Asian chip stocks. Any sign of a BIS inquiry would be a fresh catalyst.

---

data.title: Some analysts now see BoJ rates at 2.5% by mid-2027, despite slower underlying inflation
data.description:
A 2.5% BoJ path is far from priced, so the forecast is more a marker of upside risk than a market mover. If the coming months show underlying inflation turning higher, front-end JGB yields would be the first to reprice, with the yen likely to follow. The view also raises the stakes for the BoJ’s December 18 statement and Ueda’s press conference, where any hint of a faster pace would carry weight. With energy and imported costs feeding producer prices, oil and USD/JPY remain the key inputs to watch.

---
